sources.citation: Thurgood, Graham & Randy J. LaPolla (eds). 2003. The Sino-Tibetan Languages. London: Routledge (T&F e-Library ed. 2006).
sources.note: Checked the archive.org scanned text of the volume to test whether it contains a Lalo chapter: it does not (Part 4 Lolo-Burmese = Burmese, Lahu, Lisu, Akha only; Lalo mentioned once in Bradley's Lisu chapter citing Björverud 1998). Not saved (irrelevant).

sources.citation: Yang, Cathryn. 2015. Lalo dialects across time and space: subgrouping, dialectometry, and intelligibility. Asia-Pacific Linguistics A-PL 22. Canberra: Australian National University. 260 pp. (hdl 1885/95391, open access)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: No statement of stress placement. Ch. 3 gives phonological sketches of 15 Lalo varieties (Central = CW-QY, CE-YA, C-CJ, C-LJ [Longjie = Björverud's variety]) in terms of initials, rhymes, tone (3 pitch heights) and phonation (modal/breathy/harsh); syllable template (C)VTP and NT. The only mention of stress is incidental, p.39 (sec. 3.2, CW-QY): 'Following a stressed syllable, the syllabic nasal loses its syllabicity and merges with the previous syllable, as in yesterday /a²n̩³³/ > [aŋ³³].' a full-text search for stress/accent/prominence/iambic/trochaic found nothing else.

sources.note: The only reference grammar of exactly this variety (Longjie, Wuyin, Weishan = xish1235); its phonology chapter (syllable, tone, phonation) is the place a stress/accent statement would be; Yang 2015 calls it 'the most complete description of a Central Lalo variety'. A HathiTrust in-volume search for 'stress' from an unblocked browser would show in one minute whether and on which pages it discusses stress.
